records.topic: What If Jupiter's Great Red Spot Vanished?
records.secondBeat: It once stretched 40,000 kilometres, three Earths wide.
records.scientificMechanism: a long-lived anticyclone persists because Jupiter has no solid surface to create friction, but it can still shrink
records.scenarioChange: the Great Red Spot kept shrinking until it disappeared
records.expectedConsequence: Jupiter would lose its signature storm while its banded weather carried on
records.coreQuestion: If Jupiter's Great Red Spot vanished, what would it tell us about giant storms?
records.misconception: The Great Red Spot isn't fixed; it has been shrinking for over a century.
visualScenes: size comparison with Earth over time
wind speed arrows around the storm
editorialTitles: Why Jupiter's Great Red Spot Is Shrinking
What If Jupiter Lost Its Giant Storm

facts.claim: In 2004 its length was about half that of a century earlier, when it reached a size of 40,000 km (25,000 mi), about three times the diameter of Earth.
Measuring 16,350 km (10,160 mi) in width as of 3 April 2017, the Great Red Spot is 1.3 times the diameter of Earth.
Located 22 degrees south of Jupiter's equator, it produces wind speeds up to 496 km/h (308 mph).
A 2024 study suggests the permanent spot observed from 1665 to 1713 may not be the same as the modern Great Red Spot observed since 1831.

narration.text: Why Jupiter's 16,350-kilometre storm keeps shrinking.
It once stretched 40,000 kilometres, three Earths wide.
That was the Great Red Spot's width in 2017.
That's still 1.3 times Earth's diameter.
Its winds reach 496 kilometres per hour.
It's been watched continuously since 1831.
If it faded, Jupiter would lose its most famous storm, not its weather.
So even a planet-sized storm isn't permanent.

records.topic: What If Earth Became Tidally Locked to the Moon?
records.hook: Earth's day was once only 6 hours long.
records.openingLine: Earth's day was once only 6 hours long.
records.secondBeat: The Moon's tides have been slowing us ever since.
records.scientificMechanism: tidal friction transfers Earth's spin to the Moon's orbit, slowly lengthening the day
records.scenarioChange: Earth's rotation slowed until it matched the Moon's orbit
records.expectedConsequence: days lasting weeks and a Moon fixed over one hemisphere
records.coreQuestion: If Earth became tidally locked to the Moon, how long would a day last?
records.misconception: Tides don't just move oceans; they have been braking Earth's spin for billions of years.
visualScenes: Earth and Moon with tidal bulges
day length growing from 6 to 24 hours
editorialTitles: What If the Moon Stopped Earth's Spin
Why Earth's Days Keep Getting Longer

facts.claim: Tidal influence has helped lengthen the Earth day from about 6 hours to the current 24 hours (over about 4.5 billion years).
Earth's sidereal day would eventually have the same length as the Moon's orbital period, about 47 times the length of the Earth day at present.
About 59 percent of the Moon's total surface may be seen with repeated observations from Earth, due to the phenomena of libration and parallax.
Most of the far side of the Moon was not seen until 1959, when photographs were transmitted from the Soviet spacecraft Luna 3.

narration.text: Earth's day was once only 6 hours long.
The Moon's tides have been slowing us ever since.
Over 4.5 billion years, days stretched to 24 hours.
Eventually, Earth's day could match the Moon's orbit.
That's about 47 times today's day.
Then the Moon would hang over one hemisphere forever.
The Moon already shows us about 59% of its surface.
So tides aren't just ocean motion. They're a brake on the planet.

records.topic: What If Space Junk Started a Chain Reaction?
records.hook: Why one crash in orbit could close space.
records.openingLine: Why one crash in orbit could close space.
records.secondBeat: Scientists call this cascade the Kessler syndrome.
records.scientificMechanism: each collision in orbit creates fragments that raise the odds of further collisions
records.scenarioChange: debris density in low Earth orbit passed a runaway threshold
records.expectedConsequence: a collisional cascade that could make some orbits unusable for years
records.coreQuestion: If space junk started a chain reaction, could we lose access to orbit?
records.misconception: Space isn't empty around Earth; debris counts were long underestimated.
visualScenes: size of trackable versus untrackable debris
editorialTitles: The Space Junk Chain Reaction
Why One Collision Could Close an Orbit

facts.claim: The Kessler syndrome describes a situation in which the density of objects in low Earth orbit becomes so high that collisions between these objects cascade, exponentially increasing the amount of space debris over time.
In 1978, Kessler found that 42 percent of cataloged debris was the result of 19 events, primarily explosions of spent rocket stages.
Optical telescopes and short-wavelength radar measurements demonstrated that the published population count was at least 50% too low.
The list could not easily account for objects under 20 cm (8 in) in size.

narration.text: Why one crash in orbit could close space.
Scientists call this cascade the Kessler syndrome.
Kessler proposed it in 1978.
Then, 42% of tracked debris came from just 19 events.
Radar later showed debris counts were at least 50% too low.
Objects under 20 centimetres were hard to track at all.
A runaway cascade could make some orbits unusable for years.
So the biggest threat to satellites may be other satellites.

records.hook: Voyager 1 is 25.6 billion kilometres from Earth.
records.openingLine: Voyager 1 is 25.6 billion kilometres from Earth.
records.secondBeat: Its signals take nearly a day to arrive.
records.scientificMechanism: a probe coasting on its launch and gravity-assist speed keeps receding from the Sun indefinitely
records.scenarioChange: a traveller rode along on Voyager 1
records.expectedConsequence: a view of the Sun shrinking to a bright star, with messages taking nearly a day each way
records.coreQuestion: If you rode Voyager 1, what would you see, and how long would a message home take?
records.misconception: Voyager 1 hasn't left the Solar System's gravity; it has left the Sun's heliosphere.
editorialTitles: The Farthest Journey Humans Ever Sent
Why Voyager's Messages Take Almost a Day

facts.claim: Voyager 1 is a space probe launched by NASA on September 5, 1977.
At a distance of 171.19 AU (25.6 billion km; 15.9 billion mi) as of August 2026, it is the most distant human-made object from Earth.
Voyager 1 is projected to reach a distance of one light day from Earth in November 2026.
Voyager 1 crossed the heliopause and entered interstellar space on August 25, 2012, making it the first spacecraft to do so.

narration.text: Voyager 1 is 25.6 billion kilometres from Earth.
Its signals take nearly a day to arrive.
It launched on September 5, 1977.
In 2012, it became the first craft in interstellar space.
It's the most distant human-made object.
By November 2026, it will be one light-day away.
Riding along, you'd see the Sun as just a bright star.
So our farthest traveller has barely left the Sun's neighbourhood.

records.topic: What If You Spent a Summer in Death Valley?
records.secondBeat: It's the highest reliable temperature recorded there.
records.scientificMechanism: a deep, dry basin traps heat, and nights stay hot, so the body never gets to recover
records.scenarioChange: a person stayed through a Death Valley summer
records.expectedConsequence: relentless day-and-night heat that makes water and shade a matter of survival
records.coreQuestion: If you spent a summer in Death Valley, what would your body face?
records.misconception: The famous 1913 record is disputed; the reliable high is 54.4 °C.
editorialTitles: What a Summer in Death Valley Does to You
Why Death Valley's Nights Are the Real Danger

facts.claim: The highest reliable temperature in Death Valley is 130 °F (54.4 °C) recorded at Furnace Creek on August 16, 2020 and July 9, 2021.
Some modern meteorologists now dispute the accuracy of the 1913 temperature measurement due to regional mismatch and observer issues.
Summer nights provide little relief: overnight lows may dip just into the 82 to 98 °F (28 to 37 °C) range.
The greatest number of consecutive days with a maximum temperature of at least 100 °F (38 °C) was 154, in the summer of 2001.

narration.text: Death Valley hit 54.4 °C in 2020.
It's the highest reliable temperature recorded there.
The famous 1913 record is now disputed.
Summer nights often stay between 28 and 37 °C.
In 2001, it logged 154 straight days of at least 38 °C.
Without shade and water, heat stroke comes quickly.
Your body cools by sweating, and dry air speeds it up.
So the danger isn't one hot afternoon. It's heat that never breaks.

records.hook: One lake holds 19% of unfrozen fresh water.
records.openingLine: One lake holds 19% of unfrozen fresh water.
records.secondBeat: Lake Baikal, in Siberia, is also the world's oldest.
records.scientificMechanism: an active continental rift keeps deepening a basin that has collected water for millions of years
records.expectedConsequence: a fifth of Earth's unfrozen fresh water gone, and an ancient ecosystem lost
records.coreQuestion: If Lake Baikal drained, how much of the world's fresh water would vanish?
records.misconception: The world's fresh surface water isn't spread evenly; one lake holds about a fifth of it.
visualScenes: Lake Baikal from above in winter
editorialTitles: The Lake Holding a Fifth of Earth's Fresh Water
What If Lake Baikal Disappeared

facts.claim: It is estimated that the lake contains around 19% of the unfrozen fresh water on the planet.
It is also the world's oldest lake at 25–30 million years, and among the clearest.
In geological terms, the rift is young and active; it widens about 4 mm (0.16 in) per year.
The lake is divided into three basins: North, Central, and South, with depths about 900 m, 1,600 m, and 1,400 m, respectively.
In the deepest parts of the lake, from about 300 m, the temperature is stable at 3.1–3.4 °C with only minor annual variations.

narration.text: One lake holds 19% of unfrozen fresh water.
Lake Baikal, in Siberia, is also the world's oldest.
It formed 25 to 30 million years ago.
Its rift still widens about 4 millimetres a year.
Its basins reach 900, 1,600 and 1,400 metres deep.
Below 300 metres, it stays at 3.1 to 3.4 °C year-round.
Drain it, and a fifth of Earth's unfrozen fresh water disappears.
So one Siberian rift holds a startling share of our fresh water.

records.topic: What If a Tsunami Crossed an Entire Ocean?
records.hook: One earthquake ruptured 1,300 kilometres of seafloor.
records.openingLine: One earthquake ruptured 1,300 kilometres of seafloor.
records.secondBeat: The shaking lasted at least ten minutes.
records.scientificMechanism: a megathrust rupture lifts the seafloor along its whole length, launching waves across the ocean basin
records.scenarioChange: a magnitude-9 rupture struck beneath a populous ocean
records.expectedConsequence: waves reaching distant coasts hours later, deadliest where no warning exists
records.coreQuestion: If a tsunami crossed an entire ocean, what would decide how many people survive?
records.misconception: Tsunami deaths depend less on wave height than on whether a warning arrives in time.
visualScenes: fault rupture along the Sunda megathrust
wave radiating across the Indian Ocean
editorialTitles: The Tsunami That Crossed an Ocean
Why Warning Time Decides Tsunami Deaths

facts.claim: The northern section of the Sunda megathrust ruptured over a length of 1,300 km (810 mi).
facts.source: Wikipedia — 2004 Indian Ocean earthquake and tsunami

facts.claim: It had the longest fault rupture ever observed, between 1,200 to 1,300 kilometres, and had the longest duration of faulting ever observed, lasting at least ten minutes.
facts.source: Wikipedia — 2004 Indian Ocean earthquake and tsunami

facts.claim: A 2016 study estimated the magnitude to be Mw9.25, while a 2021 study revised its 2007 estimate of Mw9.1 to a new magnitude of Mw9.2; more recent studies estimate Mw9.3.
facts.source: Wikipedia — 2004 Indian Ocean earthquake and tsunami

facts.claim: The earthquake caused a massive tsunami with waves up to 30 m (100 ft) high.
facts.source: Wikipedia — 2004 Indian Ocean earthquake and tsunami

facts.claim: According to the final report of the Tsunami Evaluation Coalition, a total of 227,898 people died.
facts.source: Wikipedia — 2004 Indian Ocean earthquake and tsunami

facts.claim: The compressional (P) wave takes about 22 minutes to reach the other side of the planet.
facts.source: Wikipedia — 2004 Indian Ocean earthquake and tsunami

narration.text: One earthquake ruptured 1,300 kilometres of seafloor.
The shaking lasted at least ten minutes.
Its magnitude is estimated at 9.1 to 9.3.
Waves reached up to 30 metres high.
In total, 227,898 people died across the Indian Ocean.
Seismic waves crossed the planet in about 22 minutes.
The Indian Ocean had no tsunami warning system then.
So the deadliest part of a tsunami is the time without warning.

records.topic: What If the Continents Merged Again?
records.hook: Why the Atlantic may vanish in 250 million years.
records.openingLine: Why the Atlantic may vanish in 250 million years.
records.secondBeat: The continents could fuse into Pangaea Proxima.
records.scientificMechanism: seafloor spreading and subduction move continents in a supercontinent cycle over hundreds of millions of years
records.scenarioChange: the continents reassembled into a new supercontinent
records.expectedConsequence: a closed Atlantic and a vast interior far from any ocean
records.coreQuestion: If the continents merged again, what would the new supercontinent look like?
records.misconception: Today's map isn't permanent; continents have merged and split repeatedly.
editorialTitles: What If the Continents Merged Again
The Supercontinent Waiting in Earth's Future

facts.claim: In keeping with the supercontinent cycle, Pangaea Proxima could form within the next 250 million years.
About 125 million years from now, the Atlantic Ocean is predicted to stop widening and to begin to shrink, as seafloor spreading gives way to subduction.
Rifts will form, and Pangaea Proxima will split up once more in 400 to 500 million years.
Research published in 2022 supports an Amasia scenario within 200 to 300 million years.

narration.text: Why the Atlantic may vanish in 250 million years.
The continents could fuse into Pangaea Proxima.
In about 125 million years, the Atlantic stops widening.
Its seafloor would then start sinking back into Earth.
Another study favours a merger across the Pacific, within 200 to 300 million years.
Either way, it could split again after 400 to 500 million years.
Its interior would sit thousands of kilometres from any ocean.
So the map you know is one frame in a slow cycle.

records.topic: What If Glass Really Were a Slow Liquid?
records.hook: Why glass flows just 1 nanometre per billion years.
records.openingLine: Why glass flows just 1 nanometre per billion years.
records.secondBeat: Old church windows didn't sag because of it.
records.scientificMechanism: glass is an amorphous solid; its viscosity at room temperature is so high that flow is immeasurably slow
records.scenarioChange: window glass flowed noticeably over centuries
records.expectedConsequence: it doesn't: calculated flow is about a nanometre per billion years
records.coreQuestion: If glass were a slow liquid, would old windows sag?
records.misconception: Old windows aren't thicker at the bottom because glass flowed; it was how they were made.
editorialTitles: Is Glass Really a Liquid?
Why Old Windows Aren't Melting

facts.claim: A 2017 study computed the rate of flow of the medieval glass used in Westminster Abbey from the year 1268.
The study authors calculated that the maximum flow rate of medieval glass is 1 nm per billion years, making it impossible to observe in a human timescale.
Glassmaking dates back at least 6000 years, long before humans had discovered how to smelt iron.
Its high melting temperature (1723 °C) and viscosity make it difficult to work with.

narration.text: Why glass flows just 1 nanometre per billion years.
Old church windows didn't sag because of it.
A 2017 study checked glass in Westminster Abbey from 1268.
Even at its most fluid, that flow is far too slow to see.
Uneven panes came from how the glass was made and fitted.
Glass-making is at least 6,000 years old.
Pure silica only melts at 1,723 °C.
So glass is a solid, just one without a crystal pattern.

records.topic: What If You Cooked Pasta on a Mountain?
records.hook: At 2,438 metres, water boils at just 92 °C.
records.openingLine: At 2,438 metres, water boils at just 92 °C.
records.secondBeat: Lower air pressure lets it boil sooner.
records.scientificMechanism: water boils when its vapour pressure matches air pressure, which falls with altitude
records.scenarioChange: a cook boiled water high in the mountains
records.expectedConsequence: water boils below 100 °C, so food cooks more slowly
records.coreQuestion: If you cooked pasta on a mountain, why would it take longer?
records.misconception: Boiling water isn't always 100 °C; at altitude it boils cooler.
visualScenes: pot boiling on a mountain stove
editorialTitles: Why Water Boils Cooler on Mountains
The Physics of Cooking at Altitude

facts.claim: At 2,438.4 metres (8,000 ft) in elevation, water boils at just 92 °C (198 °F).
For every 152.4-metre (500 ft) increase in elevation, water's boiling point is lowered by approximately 1°F.
The effect starts to become relevant at altitudes above approximately 2,000 feet (610 m).
Water boils at temperatures significantly below 100 °C and, without the use of a pressure cooker, may leave boiled foods undercooked.

narration.text: At 2,438 metres, water boils at just 92 °C.
Lower air pressure lets it boil sooner.
Boiling drops about 1 °F for every 152.4 metres you climb.
The effect matters above roughly 610 metres.
Water that boils cooler cooks food more slowly.
So pasta and eggs can stay undercooked at altitude.
Pressure cookers fix this by raising the pressure again.
So a boiling pot is really a barometer.

records.topic: What If Your Brain Used Less Energy?
records.hook: Your brain uses 20% of your body's energy.
records.openingLine: Your brain uses 20% of your body's energy.
records.secondBeat: Yet it's only about 2% of your weight.
records.scientificMechanism: neurons constantly spend energy maintaining the electrical gradients that let them fire
records.scenarioChange: the brain's energy budget were cut
records.expectedConsequence: thinking and attention would suffer first
records.coreQuestion: If your brain used less energy, what would you lose?
records.misconception: The brain isn't idle at rest; it burns energy constantly.
visualScenes: blood flow to the brain diagram
resting person with active brain scan
editorialTitles: Why Your Brain Burns So Much Energy
The Most Expensive Organ in Your Body

facts.claim: The brain consumes up to 20% of the energy used by the human body, more than any other organ.
Although the human brain represents only 2% of the body weight, it receives 15% of the cardiac output, 20% of total body oxygen consumption, and 25% of total body glucose utilization.
There are more than 86 billion neurons in the brain, and a more or less equal number of other cells.
The human brain consumes approximately 60% of blood glucose in fasted, sedentary individuals.

narration.text: Your brain uses 20% of your body's energy.
Yet it's only about 2% of your weight.
It holds more than 86 billion neurons.
It takes 15% of the heart's output.
In a fasted, resting body, it consumes about 60% of blood glucose.
Much of that energy keeps neurons ready to fire.
Starve it briefly, and thinking suffers first.
So your most expensive organ is the one doing the thinking.

records.topic: What If You Could Read Your Own DNA?
records.secondBeat: Most cells carry two copies, about 6.2 billion.
records.scientificMechanism: the genome is a sequence of base pairs; only a small fraction codes for proteins
records.scenarioChange: a person read their full genome
records.expectedConsequence: billions of letters, of which only a small share are protein-coding genes
records.coreQuestion: If you could read your own DNA, how much of it would be genes?
records.misconception: Most of your DNA isn't protein-coding genes.
visualScenes: letters scrolling A C G T
editorialTitles: What Your DNA Actually Says
Why Most of Your Genome Isn't Genes

facts.claim: The total amount of DNA in this reference genome is 3.1 billion base pairs.
Most human cells are diploid so they contain twice as much DNA (~6.2 billion base pairs).
The human reference genome contains somewhere between 19,000 and 20,000 protein-coding genes.
These genes contain an average of 10 introns and the average size of an intron is about 6 kb (6,000 bp).
The human Y chromosome, consisting of 62,460,029 base pairs, was sequenced completely in January 2022.

narration.text: Your genome has 3.1 billion letters.
Most cells carry two copies, about 6.2 billion.
Yet only 19,000 to 20,000 genes make proteins.
An average gene holds about 10 introns.
The Y chromosome was only fully sequenced in January 2022.
It holds 62,460,029 base pairs.
Reading it is now routine, but understanding it isn't.
So the real mystery is what most of your DNA does.

records.topic: What If We Knocked an Asteroid Off Course?
records.hook: Why one crash moved an asteroid by 32 minutes.
records.openingLine: Why one crash moved an asteroid by 32 minutes.
records.secondBeat: NASA's DART hit Dimorphos on purpose in 2022.
records.scientificMechanism: a kinetic impactor transfers momentum to an asteroid, changing its orbit slightly
records.scenarioChange: a spacecraft rammed an asteroid on purpose
records.expectedConsequence: a measurable orbit change that, given years of warning, could steer a threat away
records.coreQuestion: If we knocked an asteroid off course, how much could one spacecraft move it?
records.misconception: Deflection isn't blowing an asteroid up; it's a small nudge applied early.
editorialTitles: The Day We Moved an Asteroid
How DART Proved Planetary Defence Works

facts.claim: The target asteroid, Dimorphos, is a 525 feet (160 m) wide moonlet of the asteroid Didymos.
The DART spacecraft collided with Dimorphos at 14,000 mph (23,000 km/h) on 26 September 2022.
The collision shortened Dimorphos's orbit around Didymos by 32 minutes, greatly in excess of the pre-defined success threshold of 73 seconds.
The spacecraft cost US$330 million by the time it collided with Dimorphos in 2022.

narration.text: Why one crash moved an asteroid by 32 minutes.
NASA's DART hit Dimorphos on purpose in 2022.
The target was a 160-metre moonlet of Didymos.
DART struck at about 23,000 kilometres per hour.
Success needed a change of just 73 seconds.
The mission cost about $330 million.
A real threat would need years of warning to nudge in time.
So planetary defence works, if we see the asteroid early.

records.topic: What If We Built a Base on the Moon?
records.hook: Humans flew around the Moon again in 2026.
records.openingLine: Humans flew around the Moon again in 2026.
records.secondBeat: Artemis II carried four astronauts on a lunar flyby.
records.scientificMechanism: a permanent base needs regular landings to deliver crews, supplies and equipment
records.scenarioChange: humans established a permanent lunar base
records.expectedConsequence: a supply chain stretching to the Moon, rehearsing life beyond Earth
records.coreQuestion: If we built a base on the Moon, what would be the hardest part?
records.misconception: The hardest part of a Moon base isn't landing once; it's supplying it continuously.
visualScenes: lunar lander on the south pole
editorialTitles: What It Takes to Live on the Moon
Why a Moon Base Is a Supply Chain

facts.claim: Artemis II sent four astronauts on a lunar flyby in 2026, becoming the only crewed flight beyond low Earth orbit not part of the Apollo program.
The uncrewed Artemis I mission sent an Orion spacecraft to lunar orbit in 2022.
Artemis IV, targeted for 2028, is planned to be the first crewed lunar landing since Apollo.
Beginning with Artemis V, NASA intends yearly lunar landings to develop a permanent lunar base, as a step toward human missions to Mars.

narration.text: Humans flew around the Moon again in 2026.
Artemis II carried four astronauts on a lunar flyby.
Artemis IV, targeted for 2028, aims to land a crew.
From Artemis V, NASA plans yearly landings.
The goal is a permanent base, then Mars.
Every kilogram of supplies must be launched or made on site.
So a Moon base is really a supply chain problem.
The Moon becomes a rehearsal for living farther away.

records.topic: What If GPS Went Dark for a Day?
records.hook: GPS clocks gain 38 microseconds a day from relativity.
records.openingLine: GPS clocks gain 38 microseconds a day from relativity.
records.secondBeat: Without correction, positions would drift quickly.
records.scientificMechanism: GPS receivers compute position from precise satellite clock signals, which also serve as a timing reference
records.scenarioChange: GPS signals stopped for a day
records.expectedConsequence: navigation falls back to other sources, while timing-dependent networks start to drift
records.coreQuestion: If GPS went dark for a day, what would fail besides your maps?
records.misconception: GPS isn't just navigation; many networks use it as a clock.
editorialTitles: What Happens If GPS Goes Dark
Why GPS Is the World's Hidden Clock

facts.claim: Relativity predicted that the clocks on GPS satellites, as observed by those on Earth, run 38 microseconds faster per day than those on the Earth.
The prototype spacecraft was launched in 1978 and the full constellation of 24 satellites became operational in 1993.
When Selective Availability was discontinued, GPS was accurate to about 5 meters (16 ft).
As of March 2026, 21 GPS satellites broadcast L5 signals.

narration.text: GPS clocks gain 38 microseconds a day from relativity.
Without correction, positions would drift quickly.
The system became fully operational in 1993.
It was designed around 24 satellites.
Civil accuracy reached about 5 metres.
If it went dark, phones would lean on cell towers and Wi-Fi.
But networks and markets that use GPS timing would feel it too.
So GPS isn't just maps. It's the world's shared clock.
